source: FAO Regional Office for Asia and the Pacific, Swine Health Management, Volume 2: Guide to Prevent and Control Porcine Reproductive and Respiratory Syndrome (RAP Publication 2012/27, Bangkok, 2012)
text: Vaccination can help protect pigs from getting seriously sick with PRRS, but it does not stop them from being infected or from spreading the virus to other pigs — vaccinated animals can still shed the virus. Modified live virus (MLV) vaccines tend to work better than killed vaccines, but they should not be used in herds that are PRRS-free, in pregnant sows and gilts, or in breeding-age boars, because the vaccine virus itself can infect unborn piglets and cause stillbirths or weak piglets, and vaccinated boars can pass the vaccine virus through their semen. A vaccination plan should be designed for the specific farm's situation rather than following a generic schedule.
caveat: Vaccine products, availability, and registration vary by country. Farmers should consult a licensed veterinarian or the local animal health authority before starting or changing a vaccination program, rather than self-administering vaccines based on this general description.
